correctness.rationale: The operative definition in Finding line 5 puts the selected vertex on a geodesic through one of the two vertices with the other as an endpoint. It does not make the selected vertex an endpoint, so it counts a selected interior point between the pair. On that literal definition the set of all original vertices qualifies: when one of the pair is original, select that endpoint; otherwise an original vertex lies inside a shortest path between the distinct subdivision vertices. But that set misses both ends of every Kneser edge (and at n=5 its size is 5, less than the claimed dimension 6). The theorem and supplied geodesic checker instead use the standard definition: d(z,x)=d(z,y)+d(y,x) or d(z,y)=d(z,x)+d(x,y). Under that intended endpoint convention the mathematics checks out. Disjoint subdivision pairs are at diameter four. For each non-disjoint case a neighbor farther from the other endpoint is immediate: use an incident subdivision with a fresh index for original–original or original–subdivision pairs, and the nonshared original endpoint for intersecting subdivision pairs. MMD pairs must be covered, and extending a geodesic at either end to a maximal one gives the converse. Intersecting edge families either share a center or consist of the triangle determined by two adjacent edges and a third avoiding their center. This gives the stated polynomial and minimal covers, and the exchange graph follows by intersections of the omitted families. Correcting the definition would not resolve the separate coverage finding below.
residual_risks: Independent direct checks exhaust n=4,5 only, for the intended standard definition: 432 and 2432 total sets respectively, 8 and 5 minimum sets, and (threshold, diameter) of (1,3) and (3,1). The failure concerns the frozen definition as written, not those conventional calculations.

evidence: From the explicit cover classification, every omitted subdivision family is a subset of a full star or triangle and original vertices can be independently selected. Size ≥2 star subsets have a unique center, and the only nonstar subsets are the complete triangles. Thus one binomial coefficient per center gives the full enumerator. For n≥5 the only minima are star complements, so each pair requires n−2 replacements because two stars share exactly one edge. At n=4 the Kneser graph is three disjoint edges; a minimum cover selects exactly one endpoint of each edge, and a budget-one move flips exactly one of those three bits.
